title: 3-Read Friday #48: Low Participation Tasks, Curriculum for Excellence, and a Do Now Routine
author: Craig Barton
summary: This issue centers on cognitive engagement, from the task level up to national curriculum design. Barton opens with Peter Foster's challenge to two activities teachers assume are engaging, note-taking and reading, arguing they often produce far less thinking than they appear to. He follows with Bruce Robertson's critique of Scotland's Curriculum for Excellence, recommending it to any reader who has heard the criticisms secondhand but never worked through the underlying argument. He closes with Dylan Kane's post on a Do Now routine, timed well for Barton, who says he was already deep in his own thinking about Do Nows, and singles out Kane's use of mini-whiteboards and variety of question types for praise.
points: Barton foregrounds cognitive engagement, not just activity type, as the lens for evaluating whether note-taking and reading are actually doing their job.
He recommends Robertson's Curriculum for Excellence critique specifically to readers who know the reputation of the criticism but not its substance.
He notes the personal timing of Kane's Do Now post, saying it landed exactly when he was already deep in his own thinking on the topic.
He calls out Kane's specific technique choices, mini-whiteboards and varied question types, as the standout features worth adopting.
quotes: Asking yourself how cognitively engaged students are at various points of your lesson is a really useful thing to do.
Here, Pete tackles head-on two common activities - note-taking and reading - suggesting they may not be as cognitively engaging as we might hope.
If you have heard the criticisms over the past few years about the Scottish curriculum but have not fully gotten to grips with the issues, this post is for you.
I am thinking a lot about Do Nows at the moment, so this from Dylan has come at a perfect time.
I like the use of mini-whiteboards (obviously), but also the consideration of the different types of questions that could be asked.
